https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cew9.text: Figure caption, Watch: Activist explains app that maps Flock camera locations By Ellie House Reporting from Houston, Texas Published 59 minutes ago Houston's historic Old Braeswood neighbourhood is affluent and tree-lined. These are not the kind of streets where you would expect to see coordinated vandalism. Yet here four surveillance cameras were attacked and cut down in the middle of the night. The metal poles were severed, leaving the distinctive black oval cameras and accompanying solar panels lying on the ground. On some of the cameras was a red sign reading: "Notice. 24/7 video recording". These cameras are run by a company called Flock Safety and this sabotage, which happened in late July, is a signal of growing concern over the nationwide spread of sophisticated AI-powered surveillance systems. Similar vandalism incidents have occurred in Minnesota, California, and Georgia. Proponents say they have made communities safer, and helped dramatically increase the rate at which crimes are solved. But recent examples of misuse have led some to worry. Critics say the cameras, which take pictures of the rear of every car that drives past, are overly broad investigative tools that treat civilians like suspects. They see the little black poles popping up in their neighbourhoods as visible reminders of state power, at a time when public confidence in institutions is historically low and many are concerned about the accelerating pace of technological change and the influence of AI on people's lives. Listen: âBig Surveillanceâ, Flock and ICE A new age of surveillance Founded in 2017, Flock Safety has become one of the country's biggest makers of Automatic Licence Plate Readers (ALPRs). These AI-powered cameras take a picture of the rear of every car that drives past. Footage is retained for a specified amount of time. But little is known about the extent that Flock is being used - the company does not publish exact data, but says it works with more than 7,000 communities nationwide, and estimates there are approximately 100,000 cameras deployed. Records obtained by the BBC provide a rare glimpse into the extensive network of cameras and surveillance tech being used in America's fourth largest city, Houston, including the use of controversial facial recognition software powered by artificial intelligence. Flock is not just selling cameras - it is selling access to a database that can include thousands of cameras from around the country. Older ALPRs did not have this vast network, which is a major selling point for law enforcement. For example, Houston's METRO Transit Authority owns 35 cameras. But documents show METRO has access to around 20,000 devices in the Flock network - including some as far as Albany County, New York. And as Flock expands, so too can the scope of investigations. Documents released to the BBC show how the network has grown year on year. In the Cypress-Fairbanks independent school district, a typical licence plate lookup in April 2024 searched around 270 networks of cameras. By April 2025, the typical search scope had almost doubled to around 500 networks. In April 2026, 20% of searches were conducted across more than 6,000 networks. Critics in Houston say this national network concerns them more than individual cameras. Christopher Rivera, from the Texas Civil Rights Project, worries that authorities could use "these databases to search our everyday routines, which ultimately scrapes out our routes to work, where our children go to school, and where we worship. And that's very problematic". Image source, Reuters Image caption, A Flock camera in Massachusetts There have been recent incidents of privacy breaches that have caught national attention. Last week, a police officer in Kentucky was charged after using the Flock system to track his ex-girlfriend - who filed a protection order - over 2,000 times. He was caught using Flock's newly mandatory, AI-powered audit tool that flags suspicious use. Others are concerned about Flock being a way for police to avoid warrants, which are usually required to search a person's property or tap their phone. In 2025, a detective in Johnson County, Texas, searched over 80,000 images to locate a woman suspected of having an abortion. He did not have a warrant. CCTV cameras, licence plate readers, and surveillance are not new. But the scale of Flock's network and the integration of AI in modern surveillance tech is a recent development and it's turned Flock into a household name. Americans who otherwise ignored the cameras in their cities have started to notice, and tune in to the capabilities of the technology around them. With AI, unlike older licence-plate readers, law enforcement can search surveillance footage with a string of words like "Caucasian man, blue shirt" - not just a licence-plate image. One thing Flock does not use is facial recognition. But that doesn't mean police departments are avoiding that tech. Critics say it violates human rights, is susceptible to misidentifying innocent people, and can be biased against minorities. The BBC has received documents revealing that Harris County Sheriff's Office, which covers Houston, uses other facial recognition technology, Clearview AI. The tool includes a database of over 70 billion images, many of which were scraped from public internet sources including social media. The documents, including purchase orders and a License Agreement, show that the county's Clearview AI contract currently runs through to March 2027. Several European countries have issued the company with data protection fines, including a Â£7.5m penalty from the UK's Information Commissioner. Harris County Sheriff's Office use of this facial recognition technology has not been reported before. The office did not respond to requests for comment. Figure caption, Police say surveillance technology like this, including Flock cameras, is important for fighting crime. "It's a very good tool," says Chief Ray Schultz of the Memorial Villages Police Department - a small jurisdiction within Houston. "It makes the community safer." Before purchasing a Flock ALPR, his department would recover an average of three stolen cars a year. Now, this figure is 45, Schultz says. Some crimes solved in recent years would have been "impossible" without Flock, he adds. Last month, Schultz used the tool to find an elderly woman with dementia who had driven 60 miles from Galveston to Houston and had got lost. "We were able to find her and reunite her with her family." Schultz says that it is important for agencies to have strong policies governing ALPR use and officers that misuse the system should be held accountable. "But don't throw out a tool that is valuable, that can help recover a missing child." 'I feel like I'm being stalked' Jasmine Khadem Gonzalez, an immigrant rights organiser, is worried that law enforcement might "use [the Flock] database to tell ICE where somebody is". The federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency does not have a contract with Flock directly. However, there have been reports of police officers citing "immigration" or "ice" as a reason for searching a licence plate. Jessie, an immigrant from Central America, noticed a Flock camera outside her house last month. She asked the BBC to not use her real name out of fear it could impact a pending case to extend her green card. "It makes me feel as if I'm being stalked," she says. In response, she's changed her commute to work: "I try to take different routes every day so there's not a pattern." But whether individual law enforcement agencies share info with the federal government is unclear. Federal immigration enforcement cannot access Flock data directly, Flock's CEO says. But some police departments have standing agreements with federal immigration enforcement to work together. In Harris County, a proposed Flock contract amendment initially included the explicit authorisation to share camera data with federal law enforcement, but this provision was later removed after push-back from campaigners. Hundreds of contracts cancelled Some jurisdictions have opted not to renew contracts with Flock as a result of these concerns, including large metropolitan areas like Los Angeles, Seattle, and Austin, Texas. In total, over 200 communities have cancelled or not renewed their contracts since 2021 - including 90 in the month of August alone - according to advocacy group Secure Justice , external . Their reasons for cancelling may include cost and concerns about data privacy. Nationally, lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have suggested there ought to be guardrails and several candidates have made it a campaign issue for the upcoming midterms. Republican Congressman Keith Self has proposed legislation that would require federal agencies to get warrants before accessing Flock data. The company itself has also amended some of its policies, such as requiring mandatory audits, and reducing the default period that data stays on a server from 30 days to 7 days, unless flagged as part of an investigation. But individual agencies can choose to retain data for much longer. Flock Safety's CEO and founder, Garrett Langley, told the BBC it's up to individual cities to decide how long to store data, and what information to share with whom. "I don't think a technology company should be making decisions like that," he says. "As long as it's a lawful investigation, we are not going to tell cities what laws they should or should not enforce." Flock is a safety, not surveillance, company, Langley says. Yet three patents filed between 2020 and 2025 have the word "surveillance" in the title. He boasts that the tech helped solve "about a million crimes" and helped find over 10,000 missing people. "The debate of how we build a society where safety and privacy coexist" is worth having, he says, but the ongoing vandalism is "disappointing". But there is nothing Flock or law enforcement could say to make Jessie feel at ease with this technology, she says. "I just don't trust that they're doing it to keep us safe." https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/09/10/koka.text: Menü Kereső Kóka János: Nem omlott össze a magyar egészségügy, ennél rosszabb történt, hozzászoktunk a rossz működéséhez Belföld Legfontosabb Forrás: Szinten túl Németh-Halász Nikolett Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom „Az egész egészségügyi rendszert fenekestül kell felfordítani” – mondta Kóka János, a Doktor24-csoport elnöke, korábbi gazdasági és közlekedési miniszter Krug Emíliának a Szinten túl című műsorban . Betegségmenedzsment helyett egészségmegőrzésre, kórházközpontúság helyett az alapellátás és a járóbeteg-ellátás megerősítésére van szükség. Nem omlott össze a magyar egészségügy, ennél rosszabb történt, hozzászoktunk a rossz működéséhez – véli Kóka. Politikai kampány helyett egészségnevelés A Portfolión megjelent egy hosszú véleménycikk Kóka Jánostól az egészségügy állapotáról. Kóka szerint a kormány arról beszélt, hogy évente 500 milliárddal többet költenek az egészségügyre, de azt is mondta, hogy a költést az uniós átlagra fogják felemelni. Ez a két szám egyébként nem találkozik – mondta Kóka. Ha valóban az uniós átlaghoz emelnék fel ezt az összeget, akkor az évente 1000 milliárd forint költést igényelne. „Ennek ma nem látom a forrásait.” De azért van pár ötlete, honnan tudna plusz forrást teremteni a kormány az egészségügyi többletkiadásokra. Megemlítette a cukros üdítők népegészségügyi termékadóját, amit szerinte meg lehetne emelni. Vagy ott van a hevített dohánytermékek jövedéki adója, illetve az ultrafeldolgozott élelmiszerek, amiket Magyarországon lényegében nem adóztatnak. Számításai szerint ezekkel együtt összesen 150 milliárd plusz pénzt lehetne behozni az egészségügybe. Krug Emília felhozta, hogy egy ilyen emelés ellen a kereskedők valószínűleg tiltakozni fognak, illetve a politikusok is nehezen jelentenek be adóemelést. Az egészségügyi miniszternek politikai vétójoga van, Kóka János szerint ezt kellene kihasználni. „Bátorság kell hozzá.” „Közbotrány, ami Magyarországon prevencióban van” – mondta a Doktor24 vezetője. Felhozott egy sokkoló adatot: vastagbélrákszűrés esetében az európai uniós megjelenési ráta nagyjából 50 százalékos, azaz minden második ember megy el szűrésre. Magyarországon egy adat van, ott 4,7 százalék ez a ráta, azaz kevesebb mint minden huszadik ember jelenik meg vastagbélrák szűrésen. Kóka szerint azért nem mennek el az emberek szűrésekre, mert nincs rajta elég fókusz. Szerinte ha a politikusok csak töredékét fordítanák egészségnevelésre annak az időnek, amit politikai kampányra fordítanak, lehetne formálni a tudatot. Nem lehetünk következmények nélküli ország A beszélgetésben szóba került a magán- és az állami egészségügy viszonya is. A magánegészségügy hosszú távú befektetés – mondta Kóka János. Ő a Doktor 24 céget húsz éve alapította, de állítása szerint egyetlen forintot sem vett ki belőle. A nemzetközi példákat látva szerinte hosszú távon ott lesz sikeres a magán egészségügy, ahol van mellette jól működő állami egészségügy. Ezek nem konkurens, hanem egymást kiegészítő rendszerek. „Nem vagyunk ebben ellenérdekeltek.” Kóka szerint olyan rendszer lenne ideális, ahol létezne egy alap szolgáltatási csomag a társadalombiztosításban. De mi van akkor, ha ezt az alapcsomagot mégsem tudja biztosítani az állami szolgáltató? Akkor meg kell vásárolni a piacon a magánszolgáltatóktól, mint ahogy ez sok területen van. A Tisza egészségpolitikájának eddigi, három hónapos munkájából a transzparenciát nagyon jó iránynak tartja. Külön kitért a kórházi fertőzésekre , amikben „ezrek halnak meg itthon”. Szerinte a kórházi higiénia kérdése az egyik legmegdöbbentőbb hiányosság Magyarországon, de az a baj, hogy láthatatlan. Kiemelte a szakdolgozói pálya nimbuszának emelését, amire nagyon nagy szükség van. A beszélgetés végén szóba került a kórházi ágyak helyzete is. Magyarországon 3-3,5-szer több aktív kórházi ágy van ezer főre vetítve, mint például Svédországban vagy Spanyolországban – mondta Kóka János. A kórházi ágyak kihasználtsága 60 százalék körül van, ami nem ideális. A beszélgetésben az egészségügy mellett téma volt a vállalkozók helyzete is. Kóka János szerint a külföldi befektetőknek jogbiztonságra van szükségük. Látok egy nagyon rossz folyamatot – mondta Kóka, ez pedig a vállalkozóellenesség. Vissza kellene nyerni a magabiztosságot, ahol a vállalkozó munkahelyek teremtője, nem szitokszó. Ez összefüggésben van azzal is, hogy az elmúlt években szerinte a politika túlságosan belemászott a vállalatok életébe. Erre elmesélt egy példát: 2023-ban a Doktor24 egyik befektetője egyik napról a másikra azt mondta, elmegy Magyarországról. Ezt azzal indokolta, hogy a lengyel–magyar barátság megbomlott, az ő befektetőjük egy lengyel állami tulajdonú bank, ahonnan azt a sugallatot kapták, hogy el kell menniük Magyarországról. Kóka szerint azért is van szükség elszámoltatásra itthon, hogy az elvesztett jogbiztonság megteremtődjön. Az elszámoltatással összefüggésben szóba került a Covid alatti lélegeztetőgépek beszerzésének ügye . Kóka János szerint a túlárazásnak kétféle oka lehetett: ilyen volt a piaci helyzet, a másik, hogy „ha itt valaki belenyúlt a mézesbödönbe, annak tényleg le kell törni a kezét”. Sportscage Riders Sportscage Team Schedules News Trade Dispute Top Stories Sportscage Agriculture Sask Ag Today Weather Polls Win & Events Win Concerts & Events 620 CKRM Country Cookout Shows Gloria Evans Cody Glydon Colin Lovequist Ray Alan Tonya Cherry Podcasts 620 CKRM App Apple App Store Google Play Contact Us Advertise September 8 Wheat Market Outlook By Doug Falconer Sep 9, 2026 | 11:51 AM Global Wheat Market Notable Items Global Black Sea logistics remain the largest international support underneath wheat markets. Ocean-bound Russian and Ukrainian exports are severely disrupted. Russia has attempted to redirect grain through Baltic and overland channels, but replacement capacity is limited. Latvia is now proposing a 300 per cent transit tariff on Russian and Belarusian grain, potentially complicating that alternative route further. Ukraine remains heavily dependent on the Danube, where the vessel queue recently reached approximately 80 ships. Diplomatic activity has increased, but the market remains far from convinced that a Russia-Ukraine peace agreement is imminent.S. envoys travelled to both Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend and presented several proposals, but no breakthrough was reached. Russia resumed major attacks on Kyiv shortly after the envoys departed, while significant disagreements remain over territorial issues. Turkey and other countries continue to be discussed as possible hosts or intermediaries, and grain shipping could form part of future negotiations, but there is currently no agreement capable of normalizing Black Sea vessel traffic. Any genuine corridor or ceasefire agreement would remove risk premium quickly. Until then, logistics remain supportive. The global wheat market is not short of wheat in the traditional sense, but exportable supplies have become more vulnerable to disruption. With a large share of internationally competitive wheat concentrated among relatively few exporters, Russia and Ukraine being a few of the top exporters in particular, the difference between wheat existing and wheat being readily deliverable to importers has become increasingly important. The latest IGC outlook places world wheat production near 817 MMT against consumption around 826 MMT, implying another inventory drawdown. More importantly, stocks held by the major exporters are expected to decline year-over-year. Australia’s ABARES last week raised its 2026/27 Australian wheat forecast sharply to 29.9 MMT from 26.7 MMT in June after better-than-expected winter rainfall across southern growing regions. The crop is still forecast below last year’s very large harvest of 35.6 MMT, but the 3.2 MMT upward revision from June provides considerably more potential export competition than markets were anticipating earlier this summer Canada Western Canadian harvest conditions have deteriorated significantly following a widespread Prairie rainfall event over the past weekend. Saskatchewan and large portions of Alberta and Manitoba received precipitation through the weekend and into Tuesday. Official Environment Canada observations show many Saskatchewan locations receiving 50–80 mm over roughly 36 hours. Across the broader recent wet pattern, some localized areas have accumulated well over 100 mm. Saskatchewan entered the event well behind normal harvest progress. As of Aug. 31, 2026, only 18 per cent of the provincial crop had been harvested compared with the five-year average of 39 per cent. Just 20 per cent of durum, 6 per cent of spring wheat, 32 per cent of barley and 4 per cent of canola were complete. Peas and lentils were considerably further advanced, but the majority of Saskatchewan’s quality-sensitive wheat and durum crop was still standing when the current wet pattern developed. Harvest activity has now been repeatedly interrupted across broad areas since approximately Sept. 4, 2026. Canadian quality is therefore becoming at least as important as final yield. Saskatchewan’s early crop reporter estimates place hard red spring wheat near 52 bu/ac, durum near 44 bu/ac and canola near 38 bu/ac. These numbers should still be treated cautiously with relatively little representative cereal or oilseed harvest completed. From here, the market will increasingly focus on falling number and sprout damage and general grading issues in wheat and durum. The forecast is better than the past several days, but not the sustained hot-and-dry pattern producers would ideally want. Saskatchewan should see a useful drying window Wednesday and Thursday in several areas, but temperatures are forecast to cool materially afterward. As of now a meaningful portion of Prairie wheat and durum harvest could still be outstanding as the calendar moves beyond mid-September. Canadian wheat export movement has nevertheless started the new crop year exceptionally well. Through Week 4 ending August 30, exports of wheat excluding durum reached 2.00 MMT compared with 1.24 MMT at the same point last year. Durum exports reached approximately 377,000 tonnes compared with only 135,000 tonnes last year. The strong start reinforces Canada’s export competitiveness following last year’s record campaign, although ultimately there is expected to be less wheat available during 2026/27 and now with potential changes in quality, the trajectory may change. We will know more on quality of exportable crop in the coming weeks ahead. There is a heavy agricultural report calendar over the next eight days. Statistics Canada releases July 31 stocks of principal field crops on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, which will provide the final official carry-in picture for the new crop year. USDA releases its September WASDE and U.S. Crop Production reports Friday, Sept. 11, 2026, while Statistics Canada’s more important model-based August production estimates follow on Sept. 16, 2026. The Statistics Canada production report should provide a much better national benchmark for wheat, durum and canola before enough harvest information is available to fully judge this year’s crop U.S. Wheat markets remain volatile following the sharp rally of the past several weeks. Minneapolis, Kansas City and Chicago wheat gave back some geopolitical premium but have strengthened again on Tuesday, with December Minneapolis near $7.55/bu. Minneapolis remains roughly $1.50/bu above its late-June lows, reflecting a market that has shifted from relatively comfortable supply expectations toward greater concern around Black Sea logistics and, increasingly, Canadian harvest and quality risk. U.S.-China trade negotiations could become increasingly important for the broader grain and oilseed complex later this month. President Xi Jinping is scheduled to visit the United States on Sept. 24, 2026, and U.S. officials have specifically pressed China on fulfilling agricultural-purchase commitments ahead of the meeting. Focus will be on if there may be additional Chinese demand for U.S. soybeans or other agricultural products and could materially influence soybean, soybean-oil and canola sentiment. Canada-U.S. trade: Canada placed retaliatory tariffs on roughly C$27.6 billion of U.S. goods took effect Tuesday, following U.S. tariffs of up to 50 per cent on approximately C$27.6 billion of Canadian goods. Importantly, current reporting indicates official negotiations have stalled and there are presently no government-level talks underway. Most Canadian grain continues to benefit from CUSMA treatment, but the escalation adds currency, input-cost and broader North American trade-policy uncertainty Market Outlook – Wheat Wheat markets enter the week with a firmer underlying tone, but Western Canadian harvest quality is becoming an increasingly important source of direction. Widespread Prairie rainfall arrived with a large share of the spring wheat crop still standing, raising the risk of overall grading issues including sprouting, falling-number issues and a wider grade spread if harvest delays persist. A meaningful deterioration in No. 1 and No. 2 CWRS availability could tighten the pool of exportable high-quality wheat and provide additional support to premiums even if overall production remains respectable. Black Sea and Sea of Azov shipping disruptions continue to underpin futures, although diplomatic regional powers are helping in negotiating some resolutions to the conflict. Stronger crop update from Australia ABARES provided a bit of a bearish offset although the increase in crop size estimates was largely expected, while U.S. spring wheat harvest results have generally been respectable. Over the next one to two weeks, Canadian protein, test weight, grade distribution and harvest progress should become increasingly representative and could have a larger influence on market direction than headline yield estimates alone. Market Outlook – Durum Durum quality risk has moved to the forefront following widespread Prairie rainfall with a large share of the Western Canadian crop still standing. If prolonged harvest delays result in lower test weight, sprouting or a larger-than-expected share of No. 3 or lower and feed-quality durum, the market could tighten quickly for exportable No. 1 and No. 2 CWAD and materially shift otherwise comfortable durum fundamentals. For now, smaller North American production continues to be offset by improved crops and weaker import requirements across North Africa and Turkey, with IGC forecasting global production near 38.9 MMT and world trade at a five-year low. Early Saskatchewan yield indications have been coming in but from a relatively small sample size leaves us wanting to see a few more yield reports yet. Grade distribution and protein will be the key variables over the next two weeks. https://www.theguardian.com/world/live/2.text: The Houthis this morning have just also issued a warning to travellers and airlines to stay away from Saudi airports following yesterday’s attack. It’s the first public message from the group since Saturday’s deadly assault. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Mecca and Medina – the holiest cities in Islam - were excepted but the other Saudi airports and airspace “are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces”. He warned the public to “take our warning seriously” and also claimed that “Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions”. The Gulf state has been asking the US and other Western allies for more missile interceptors since the fighting escalated. Saree ended his post by saying his group is pursuing: “airport for airport, siege for siege, and escalation for escalation” until they achieved their goals. All week the Houthis have been striking the main airport in the Saudi capital as Saudi Arabia has increased strikes on Houth

Photograph: Ian Patrick/Alamy Airline industry UK government promises disabled air passengers better safeguards Despite recent progress, almost a fifth of air travellers with disabilities are still dissatisfied with their experience Gwyn Topham Transport correspondent Mon 19 Oct 2026 03.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Disabled passengers will have better safeguards when flying, the government has pledged, including protection from damaged wheelchairs and support from trained staff. A report from an industry-led accessibility group said there was “much more to be done” but progress was being made, a year after a review led by Tanni Grey-Thompson demanded action to improve air travel in response to numerous incidents in which passengers had been left stranded without assistance. The Department for Transport said airports had added more staff training and a new standardised system has been set up to prepare airlines for handling mobility aids, after more than 1,000 wheelchairs were damaged in transit in 2024, equivalent to more than 80 a month. Almost one in five disabled passengers are still dissatisfied with their air travel experience though, according to an industry body, and requests for assistance are continuing to rise. The government is planning to remove the maximum payout in compensation for lost and damaged wheelchairs, and to give the aviation regulator new powers to fine airlines and airports when passengers are not given the assistance they need to travel. The changes are expected to be in the civil aviation bill which is progressing through parliament and which the government said would give air passengers stronger protection and consumer rights. The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander , said: “People must be able to fly with dignity and peace of mind. For disabled passengers this means not worrying about their wheelchair coming back in one piece, or whether staff will be there to support them around the airport. “We’ve backed industry to overhaul staff training, prevent damage to mobility aids and create easy, simple ways for passengers to share key information before they fly.” The co-chairs of the aviation accessibility implementation group, which is assessing progress on the 19 recommendations in Grey-Thompson’s report, said: “There is much more to be done, but we have made a positive start. We will be focusing now on embedding more of the changes that are needed to enable disabled people to fly with confidence and dignity.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion The chief executive of lobby group Airlines UK, Tim Alderslade, said the number of passengers requiring assistance was up nearly 10% year on year. “82% report that they are satisfied with their air travel experience which demonstrates the efforts and progress airlines are making for those who require additional support when they fly,” he said.
